Machine learning is now common in astronomical research because modern data are so large and complex. Astronomers now routinely work with datasets of billions of objects and petabytes of information. This holds from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to the Vera Rubin Observatory and Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. At this scale, automated analysis is necessary.

Discussions about machine learning in astronomy are often confused. The term “machine learning” has become nearly synonymous with neural networks and deep learning, which are recent and popular. But machine learning is a much broader set of techniques with a long history in statistical analysis. Treating the two as the same makes productive discussion harder than it needs to be.

Machine learning has also become a polarizing issue in the research community. Much of this comes from misconceptions about what machine learning is and how it connects to the statistical foundations that astronomers have long used. Some presentations treat the methods as “black boxes” that avoid the need for rigorous statistical thinking. This has divided researchers into those who embrace the methods and those who distrust them.

The root of the problem is how we usually present the techniques. Existing resources fall into three groups. Classical statistics textbooks are rigorous but often stop before modern methods like neural networks. Machine learning textbooks focus on implementation and give less space to the statistical foundations that make the methods valid for science. Astronomy-focused books are rare. Those that exist tend to focus on practical applications, which is a different goal from teaching the theory.

This gap matters most in astronomy, where the need for interpretability and uncertainty quantification is greater than in most other fields. Computer scientists often view statistics and machine learning differently from physical scientists. In commercial applications, predictive power often justifies the means. In astronomy, we need to know what our models predict, why they predict it, and how confident we should be in the results. Sometimes we use these techniques to question existing physical models or to claim new discoveries. Then we must be clear about what counts as statistical evidence of discovery.

The result is a fragmented approach. Researchers often learn one technique for one problem. They use clustering for galaxy classification, regression for stellar parameter estimation, and neural networks for image analysis. They may not see the statistical principles that connect these techniques. This piecemeal approach limits how well researchers use the techniques. It also feeds the perception that machine learning is only a collection of tools, without the theoretical depth of physics.

This textbook closes that gap by showing that machine learning techniques are natural extensions of the statistical methods astronomers have long used. We do not present them as revolutionary departures from older approaches. We show how they follow from the same probability theory and Bayesian inference that underlie scientific data analysis. We build this foundation step by step and give a helicopter view of the field. We hope this demystifies these techniques and helps astronomers apply them with more thought.

What is Machine Learning

Machine learning has the same goal as scientific modeling. Both try to build a coherent worldview from observed data. Newton developed the law of gravity to predict planetary positions without explicit lookup tables. In the same way, machine learning tries to learn general rules that apply to new situations. In this view, “pure learning” and “pure modeling” are the two ends of a spectrum. Real approaches lie somewhere between them.

Machine learning methods rely on inductive bias, the set of assumptions that guide learning when the data alone cannot determine a unique solution. In linear regression, we assume relationships follow hyperplanes, flat surfaces that generalize straight lines. When we choose a kernel function for a Gaussian Process, we encode beliefs about the smoothness of a function. When we design a convolutional neural network, we assume translation invariance in images. These biases are not weaknesses. Without them, learning from finite data is impossible.

Stronger assumptions let us learn efficiently from limited data, but they can reduce flexibility. This trade-off between modeling (adding assumptions) and learning (finding patterns in data) appears throughout science. Even physical theories rest on implicit assumptions about mathematical form, symmetry, and which phenomena are relevant. Machine learning makes these assumptions explicit through the choice of algorithm. It gives a principled way to balance prior knowledge against evidence from data.

This view shows why machine learning is not so different from the astronomical analysis we already do. Choosing between a parametric stellar evolution model and a neural network to predict stellar properties is a choice of position on the modeling-learning spectrum. It is not a choice between science and black-box algorithms. Both combine theory with data-driven discovery. Machine learning is most powerful when it augments scientific understanding and does not replace it.

What This Book Is and What It Is Not

This textbook is about statistical machine learning for astronomy. Its main aim is to build the theoretical foundations needed to understand these methods and apply them correctly. The book has a substantial chapter on neural networks and deep learning, but it is not mainly a deep learning textbook. We see deep learning as the natural end point of a progression that starts with basic probability theory and moves through more sophisticated statistical techniques. The theory of deep learning is still catching up with its success, much as thermodynamics came after decades of steam engines.

Our approach is deliberately “classical-centric” and puts first the statistical principles that make machine learning methods work. We have three reasons. First, classical techniques often give analytical solutions and well-understood uncertainties, which remain useful in many astronomical applications. Second, knowing these foundations shows why and when more complex methods like neural networks become necessary. Third, many supposedly “modern” techniques are natural extensions of classical ideas. This connection is easiest to see when we place both in the same statistical framework.

We use a musical analogy to frame this choice. Classical machine learning methods are like classical music. They need more initial investment to appreciate, but this foundation helps us understand more complex forms. Neural networks and deep learning are more like contemporary popular music, or K-pop. They are immediately accessible and often quite powerful, but you appreciate them more when you know some of the principles behind the music.

This book is not a survey of machine learning techniques or a handbook of implementations. We aim to build conceptual understanding and mathematical intuition, which we believe lead to better application in the end. Our goal is to develop researchers who can think critically about which methods suit which problems, and why.

We derive methods from first principles instead of presenting them as given algorithms. This makes the connections between techniques that look unrelated clear. We are unrelenting in our mathematical approach, from the uniqueness proof for MCMC to the induction proof for Principal Component Analysis. This might seem like too much, but we believe this rigor is critical for the motivation of this book. Without the theoretical foundations, we cannot judge when methods are appropriate, how they might fail, or how they fit into statistical inference. We balance this rigor with analogies, geometric interpretations, and physical intuition that show what the mathematics means.

The astronomical focus also sets this book apart from general machine learning texts. Astronomical data bring particular difficulties. These include irregular sampling, heteroscedastic uncertainties that differ from point to point, physical constraints, and the need for proper error propagation. We use astronomical examples as the central problems that motivate the techniques.

This textbook does not claim new theoretical results or new algorithms. Its mathematical foundations, statistical principles, and machine learning techniques are well established in the literature. The individual parts sit in specialist texts, research papers, and technical resources. They do not appear to be available elsewhere in one compact form. Our role is curation and pedagogical organization. We collect, connect, and present established results in one coherent framework for astronomical applications, so that researchers can build a systematic understanding.

Online Tutorials and Further Reading

Understanding comes first, but practice matters too. The companion tutorials are runnable and work through astronomical examples, many with real data. Readers who want to implement the methods should work through them as they read the matching chapters. The tutorials, and further reading for each chapter, are at https://statml.org/.

The Structure of This Textbook

The book has a planned progression that keeps a clear link to astronomical applications. The structure follows from our belief that machine learning is best understood as an extension of statistical inference, not as a separate discipline.

We begin with probability theory and, above all, Bayesian inference (Chapters 2-3). The philosophy of Bayesian inference as a framework for uncertainty quantification runs through the book. This investment in foundations pays off throughout, because it lets us show how methods that look different follow from the same principles. We then look at summary statistics, showing that finite data limit what we can learn about probability distributions. This creates the need for more sophisticated approaches.

Supervised learning (Chapters 4-9) follows a logical sequence in which complexity grows out of the limits of simpler methods. Supervised learning maps inputs to known outputs. We learn the relationship between variables from examples of both. We start with linear regression. Maximum likelihood leads to the method of least squares that readers may know from physics, and a Bayesian treatment gives uncertainty quantification. Bayesian linear regression then shows how to include prior knowledge formally, and how regularization connects to Bayesian priors.

Chapter 6 treats input uncertainties. This matters particularly in astronomy, where measurement errors in both dependent and independent variables are common. The chapter leads to the iterative optimization methods needed for logistic regression (Chapters 7-8). These in turn motivate the Bayesian treatment of classification in Chapter 9.

Unsupervised learning (Chapters 10-11) follows a similar philosophy. It looks for patterns without known target outputs and finds hidden structure rather than input-output relationships. We show how Principal Component Analysis follows from constrained optimization. We also show how K-means and Gaussian Mixture Models give related ways to find structure in data. Both rely on the expectation-maximization algorithm, a general framework for hidden variables. This development makes clear how the methods depend on their assumptions about the data.

Computational methods (Chapters 12-13) come next. As models grow more complex, we often cannot solve them analytically. Then we need sampling. Our treatment of Monte Carlo and Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods gives the numerical tools for complex probabilistic models. It stays tied to the Bayesian framework from the earlier chapters. It also prepares us for simulation-based inference at the end of the book.

Gaussian Processes (Chapter 14) join linear algebra, kernel methods, and Bayesian inference. We can view them as kernelized linear models or as distributions over functions. The same mathematics describes both. The chapter explains how a kernel defines a prior over functions and how a Gaussian Process makes predictions with uncertainties. It also shows how Gaussian Processes connect to neural networks.

Finally, neural networks (Chapter 15) appear as a natural extension of the earlier methods. Autoencoders extend Principal Component Analysis, and mixture density networks extend Gaussian Mixture Models. Neural networks give up some of the mathematical tractability and uncertainty quantification of classical methods, and gain scalability and flexibility. By this point, readers have the background to see both what neural networks can do and what limits they inherit. We show several approaches to uncertainty quantification, from Monte Carlo dropout to the Bayesian treatments available for simpler models. The chapter closes with neural density estimators and simulation-based inference, where the probability models, sampling methods, and neural networks of the earlier chapters come together.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this textbook, you will have a systematic understanding of statistical machine learning. You will be able to apply these methods to astronomical research problems with confidence. This understanding works at several levels.

At the conceptual level, you will understand how machine learning techniques follow from probability theory and Bayesian inference. This will let you judge new methods critically and understand their assumptions, limits, and proper domains of use.

At the mathematical level, you will be comfortable with the derivations and analysis of key algorithms. This includes how maximum likelihood estimation leads to specific loss functions. Mathematical understanding is the basis for confident application and troubleshooting.

At the practical level, especially with the accompanying tutorials, you will know how to match statistical techniques to astronomical problems. This includes knowing when linear models are enough and when you need more complex approaches. It includes knowing how to build physical knowledge into statistical models. It also includes knowing how to evaluate and compare different approaches to the same problem. You will also understand the computing trade-offs between methods, and how to balance statistical rigor against practical constraints.

Most important, you will learn to think statistically about astronomical problems. This means understanding how uncertainty propagates through analysis pipelines and how to tell different sources of uncertainty apart. Techniques that first seem complicated often turn out to be simple in the right framework. We hope this book gives you that framework, and that you can use it throughout your research career, whatever direction the tools take.
